text:
Nobody writes a headline about the settlement that went fine.

Thousands of them happen every week. People buy, move, refinance, restructure, and nothing about it is news.

The one that falls over gets the front page. That’s not the market. That’s how attention works.

Your home is worth less than it was last year.

If you love it, aren’t selling, and the repayments are comfortable, that number changes almost nothing about your Tuesday.

If you need to sell, or the buffer is thin, it changes everything.

Same market. Very different problems.

The financial conversation you keep putting off takes about twenty minutes.

Most people avoid it because they’re braced for bad news.

Most of the time the answer is “you’re fine, here’s the one thing to tidy up.”

What if you’re actually fine? You’d want to know that too.

You don’t need to predict the market.

You need to know three numbers.

Got a mortgage? Your rate, your buffer in months, and what one more rise does to the repayment.

Buying? Your borrowing power, before you fall for a house.

Selling? What you walk away with after the loan and the costs.

When everyone thinks property is going up, people are terrified of missing out.

When everyone thinks it’s falling, they’re terrified of making a mistake.

Same market. Different fear.

Sometimes the smart move is buying. Sometimes it’s refinancing. Sometimes it’s doing absolutely nothing. The fear should never be the one deciding.

Not every problem in the headlines needs to become a problem in your house.

Five ways to tell the difference.

None of them involve guessing what the Reserve Bank does next.

Prices falling is a headline.

Whether it’s your problem depends on one question: are you selling, struggling, or short on equity?

If none of those, it’s weather. If any of them, it’s a conversation worth having now.

A rate rise is a headline.

Your problem is a buffer you can’t measure.

Divide what you have by what one more rise costs each month. If the answer is a number of months, you have a plan. If it’s a shrug, you don’t yet.

Borrowing power shrinking is a headline.

Your number depends on which lender reads your payslips.

The same income gets different answers at different banks. Know yours before you fall for a house, not after.

Everyone refinancing is a headline.

Your loan might already be fine.

If the rate is good and a switch adds nothing structural, the smartest move is leaving it alone. Doing nothing is a decision too, when you’ve made it on purpose.
